8057a0ef9 Anchor every os.Root on a trusted base
An os.Root is only as trustworthy as the directory it is opened on, and the
wrong version of that reads as the right one:

    root, _ := osroot.Shared(filepath.Dir(target))
    data, _ := osroot.ReadFile(root, filepath.Base(target))

Every component the caller resolved sits ABOVE that root, so the containment
covers one fixed name and enforces nothing the filepath.Join had not already
decided. A symlink at .claude, at .entire, at entire-investigations is
resolved before the root exists. Anchoring one level up -- on a directory a
resolver produced -- makes those components names INSIDE the root, which is
what os.Root and MkdirAllNoSymlink can refuse.

Three call sites shipped the derived-base shape, and one of them had a
containment check that could never fire: settings.clonePreferencesRoot
computed its common dir as filepath.Dir(filepath.Dir(abs)) and handed both
to gitdir.OpenPathIn, so the relative path was correct by construction. It
now recovers the common dir by removing a compile-time constant suffix,
which fails loudly on a path of the wrong shape. contexts and discovery take
the DIRECTORY the caller chose instead of the file: configRoot(configDir),
and a cacheFile{dir, name} pair in place of a joined path.

Two roots stay anchored on their target's parent and now say why: tokenstore
($ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE_PATH) and settings' explicit-path fallback both act on
a path the CALLER named, so its parent is the caller's choice too and there
is no separate trusted base to prefer.

The seven agent hook-config trees had no root at all. Each of .claude,
.cursor, .gemini, .github/hooks, .factory, .codex and .opencode/plugin was
four lines of filepath.Join + os.MkdirAll + os.WriteFile carrying a
//nolint:gosec saying the path came from the repo root -- which describes
where the path was BUILT, not where it RESOLVES. A working tree arrives by
clone, so a repository carrying a checked-in symlink at .claude had `entire
enable` create directories and write JSON through it, outside the repository
included. agent.HookConfigFile replaces all seven with one type anchored on
the worktree root.

One behaviour change falls out of that and is pinned by a test rather than
left to be discovered: an ABSOLUTE symlink at the config FILE
(.claude/settings.json -> ~/dotfiles/...) no longer resolves, because
os.Root refuses absolute symlinks unconditionally. A relative link inside
the worktree still works, and a symlinked config DIRECTORY is now refused --
which is the point.

investigate gets the same treatment, and there it covers a sink its own
comments already warned about: StateStore.RunDir noted that an unvalidated
run id "would be a path-traversal sink" because callers feed the result to
os.RemoveAll, and clean did exactly that with two functions returning
absolute paths. Deleting now belongs to the stores, which resolve a run id
as a name inside the git common dir. Reading gets it too, closing a real
gap: LocalManifest.FindingsDoc is an absolute path decoded from a JSON file
on disk, and show plus the run footer both followed it, so a manifest could
choose which file was printed. Bootstrap no longer writes at all -- it
renders a body the caller persists through StateStore.WriteFindings.

Also rooted: the checkpoint loose-object delete; the trail worktree
checkout's .gitignore and .worktreeinclude, plus the SOURCE half of its
ignored-file copy (the destination was already rooted on the argument that
the branch content is not user-authored -- the same argument applies to the
files being read); the plugin asset download; the hook-path attribution
read, which read every file in `git status` output on a joined path; the
trail-review location reads, which went through a hand-rolled validator and
take their path from the API; and rewind's restore, which kept a
`repoRoot = "."` fallback and its own os.OpenRoot. Restoring a checkpoint
tree into whatever directory the process is sitting in is worse than not
restoring; it now fails, goes through worktreedir, and creates directories
with MkdirAllNoSymlink, which matters most there because the tree entries
may have been fetched from a remote.

agent.sessionStoreForWrite had the inverse problem: a SessionRef outside the
agent's session store fell through to a root anchored on its own parent, so
the one input that failed the containment check was the one input that
disabled it. The comment justifying that said some agents resolve a restored
session to a sibling directory; they do not -- Codex's
ResolveRestoredSessionFile nests inside the store -- so the branch was
unreachable as well as unsound. It is an error now.

1eaccf772 Give every tree Entire writes to a single os.Root anchor
Entire does filesystem I/O in six trees, and until now each read and write
assembled its own absolute path and handed it to os.ReadFile/os.WriteFile.
Containment was therefore a property each call site had to keep honouring
by hand, and several of them carried comments saying so outright:
PluginDataDir "guarantees ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR always points inside the
managed data subtree", investigate.RunDir noted that "an unvalidated id
would be a path-traversal sink" feeding os.RemoveAll.

Each tree now has one package that owns a shared *os.Root over it, and the
names that reach those roots are relative to them:

  .entire                    entiredir
  git common dir             gitdir
  the working tree           worktreedir
  an agent's session store   agent.SessionStore
  per-user config / cache    userdirs.ConfigRoot / CacheRoot
  managed plugin tree        pluginRoot

The roots memoize through one registry, osroot.Shared, replacing three
separate copies of that map. Directory creation goes through
osroot.MkdirAllNoSymlink, which refuses a component that already exists as
a symlink -- os.Root blocks a symlink that escapes a root but follows one
pointing elsewhere inside it, and an escaping one otherwise surfaces as an
opaque errno far from the cause. entire doctor reports the symlinks that
are already there.

Two anchors are worth calling out because they close a real gap rather
than formalising an existing one. agent.SessionStore is where a hook
payload's session ID becomes a path via the agent's own
ResolveSessionFile; SessionFile converts the result back to a name inside
the store and rejects an ID that walked out of it, which a plain
filepath.Join produced silently. worktreedir covers the checkpoint tree
entries rewind restores, which may have been fetched from a remote --
rewind's restore half already opened a root for that reason; the reads
beside it did not.

paths.WorktreeRoot is now the single answer to "where is the repository",
and entiredir.anchor falls back to the current directory only on git's
positive ErrNotARepository verdict. The fallback it replaces fired on any
resolve failure, `git` off $PATH included, and then silently gave an agent
working in a subdirectory of a real repo its own .entire beside itself. A
root is only as trustworthy as the directory it is opened on, so a base
that cannot be resolved is not a base to guess at.

settings.readConfined keeps its symlink refusal on every branch, through
one readConfinedIn: the .entire branch briefly read straight through
osroot.ReadFile, which follows an in-root symlink silently -- precisely
the .entire/settings.local.json -> planted.json case the check exists for.

func TestMaybeSpawnSessionSweep_SeamAndThrottle(t *testing.T) {
	// Cannot use t.Parallel(): t.Chdir and the package-level seam swap are
	// process-global.
	dir := setupGitRepoForPhaseTest(t)
	t.Chdir(dir)
	ctx := context.Background()

	var spawns atomic.Int32
	var gotRoot atomic.Value
	prevSpawn := sweepSpawn
	prevGitCommonDir := sweepGitCommonDir
	sweepSpawn = func(worktreeRoot string) {
		spawns.Add(1)
		gotRoot.Store(worktreeRoot)
	}
	t.Cleanup(func() {
		sweepSpawn = prevSpawn
		sweepGitCommonDir = prevGitCommonDir
	})

	// No zombies: no spawn (and no throttle marker written — the throttle is
	// only consulted once a zombie nominates).
	maybeSpawnSessionSweep(ctx)
	assert.Equal(t, int32(0), spawns.Load(), "no zombies must not spawn a sweep")

	old := time.Now().Add(-48 * time.Hour)
	zombie := &strategy.SessionState{
		SessionID:  "2026-08-17-spawn-seam-zombie",
		BaseCommit: testBaseCommit,
		Phase:      session.PhaseEnded,
		StepCount:  1,
		StartedAt:  old.Add(-time.Hour),
		EndedAt:    &old,
	}
	require.NoError(t, strategy.SaveSessionState(ctx, zombie))

	// A common-dir failure means there is no safe repository-wide throttle key.
	// Fail closed rather than forking an unbounded child on every session start.
	sweepGitCommonDir = func(context.Context) (string, error) {
		return "", errors.New("common dir unavailable")
	}
	maybeSpawnSessionSweep(ctx)
	assert.Equal(t, int32(0), spawns.Load(), "common-dir failure must not spawn a sweep")
	sweepGitCommonDir = prevGitCommonDir

	// Zombie present: exactly one spawn, with the worktree root.
	maybeSpawnSessionSweep(ctx)
	require.Equal(t, int32(1), spawns.Load(), "a zombie must spawn exactly one sweep")
	got, okRoot := gotRoot.Load().(string)
	require.True(t, okRoot, "seam must have been handed a worktree root")
	require.NotEmpty(t, got)
	wantRoot, err := filepath.EvalSymlinks(dir)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	gotEval, err := filepath.EvalSymlinks(got)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.Equal(t, wantRoot, gotEval, "sweep must be spawned from the worktree root")

	// Throttle marker is now fresh: the zombie still nominates, but no second
	// child is forked within the window.
	maybeSpawnSessionSweep(ctx)
	assert.Equal(t, int32(1), spawns.Load(),
		"a second session start within the throttle window must not spawn another sweep")
}

# Thermo-Nuclear Review: Consolidating Git Metadata Traversal

## Purpose

This is a local coordination note for a guided architectural review in
`entireio/cli` on branch `refactor-git-metadata-traversal`. It records the
starting thermo-nuclear verdict, verified evidence from the walkthrough, and
which findings the user has accepted.

Treat the proposed conclusions as hypotheses to challenge. A future agent must
independently inspect the current code, tests, history, and live GitHub state
before recommending or implementing changes.

No consolidation implementation had been made when this note was created.

## Trigger

- Merged PR #2052, `fix(codex): use repository hook root in linked worktrees`:
  <https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2052>
- Soph's “Fourth implementation of worktree traversal” finding:
  <https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2052#issuecomment-5400538888>
- Later commitment to broader consolidation:
  <https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2052#issuecomment-5429341093>

Prior research found overlapping answers in these symbols and areas:

- `gitrepo.ResolveDotGitPath`
- `gitrepo.ResolveCommonGitPath`
- `paths.GetWorktreeID`
- `session.GetGitCommonDir`
- `strategy.GetGitCommonDir`
- Checkpoint common-directory resolution
- Explicit-root probes
- Codex hook-root discovery

## Walkthrough cadence and current state

- Discuss exactly one material finding at a time.
- Explain it using concrete codebase examples, then stop for questions or
  confirmation.
- Do not move into patches or migration planning until the material design
  findings have been discussed and accepted.
- Do not repeat an accepted finding unless the user asks.
- Finding 1 was discussed and accepted.
- Finding 2 was presented in technical and simplified forms and then accepted.

### Walkthrough tracker

| Finding | Status | Next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 — Fragmented ownership | Accepted | None unless the user reopens it |
| 2 — Common-directory caches | Accepted | Delete only after replacing subprocess traversal |
| 3 — Resolver policy options | Accepted | Keep one fixed physical resolver contract |
| 4 — Affected giant files | Accepted | Former owner modules must become smaller |
| 5 — Compatibility wrappers | Accepted | Keep no compatibility wrappers in the final tree |
| 6 — Worktree identity | Accepted with physical-identity amendment | Preserve lexical outputs; compare physical relationship for identity |
| 7 — Genuine Git queries | Accepted | Replace only explicit-root physical traversal |
| 8 — Repository-opening fallback | Accepted | Metadata failure must remain fatal; fallback requires positive safety evidence |
| 9 — Consumer error policy | Accepted | Preserve required, warning, and fail-open behavior at owning callers |
| 10 — Bare repository boundary | Accepted | Consolidate all worktree traversal; keep bare repository opening distinct |
| 11 — Hot-path subprocess boundary | Accepted | Pass known roots directly and measure whole operations |
| 12 — Path identity boundaries | Accepted | Converge symlink aliases for equality and lock ordering only |
| 13 — Ownership enforcement | Accepted; required | Prevent new common-directory resolvers outside `gitrepo` |
| 14 — Executable design proof | Accepted | Make real Git layouts the specification and malformed fixtures explicit |
| Material design walkthrough | Complete | Await explicit implementation approval |

At the time the note was created:

- The worktree was clean before this note was added.
- The branch was 11 commits behind and 0 ahead of the locally cached
  `upstream/main`.
- The relevant metadata and cache files had no diff between the branch and that
  cached `upstream/main`.
- Live GitHub verification was started but interrupted, so re-check it.
- Entire was enabled, but the checkpoint IDs attached to the two cache commits
  were not available locally. Recorded intent below therefore comes from commit
  bodies, not checkpoint transcripts.

Live state rechecked on 2026-08-28:

- PR #2052 is merged and closed.
- After fetching current `upstream/main`, the branch is 18 commits behind and
  0 ahead. The earlier 11-commit count was stale.
- The session and checkpoint common-directory cache files remain unchanged on
  current `upstream/main`. A newer `paths.WorktreeRoot` change improves error
  classification but retains the worktree-root cache.
- This coordination note remains the only local worktree change.
- No discoverable follow-up PR or issue has superseded this consolidation.

## Thermo-nuclear verdict

The consolidation is necessary, but merely adding `WorktreeMetadata`,
preserving the existing caches, and wrapping every old function would move
complexity rather than delete it.

The proposed code-judo move is:

> Stop modeling Git layouts as special cases. Model the relationship between
> the worktree's Git directory and its common Git directory.

That relationship should naturally explain normal repositories, linked
worktrees, `.bare`, conventional bare repositories with linked worktrees,
separate Git directories, ordinary submodules, and linked submodules.

## Central model

```text
worktree root
    |
    v
<root>/.git
    | directory or gitdir pointer
    v
per-worktree Git directory
    |
    +-- no commondir ------------------+
    |                                  |
    +-- commondir pointer --> common Git directory
                                       |
                                       v
                      Is the per-worktree directory an
                   immediate child of <common>/worktrees?
                              /                  \
                            yes                  no
                             |                    |
                         linked ID          primary/ordinary
```

This would eliminate path-marker policy such as:

- Searching for `.git/worktrees/`
- Searching for `.bare/worktrees/`
- Finding the last `/modules/`
- Deciding whether `/worktrees/` appears before or after `/modules/`
- Guessing `parent(parent(dotGitDir))`

## Structural findings

### Finding 1 — Blocker: fragmented ownership of Git metadata semantics

Status: **accepted**.

The central defect is not merely duplicated code. Several packages
independently decide what `.git`, `commondir`, and worktree identity mean.
Consequently, a fix in one resolver does not propagate to the others.

The generic layer should expose physical Git facts, not a growing `GitLayout`
taxonomy such as `Normal`, `Linked`, `Bare`, `DotBare`, `SeparateGitDir`,
`Submodule`, and `LinkedSubmodule`.

Provisional fact shape:

```go
type WorktreeMetadata struct {
    DotGitDir  string
    CommonDir  string
    WorktreeID string
}
```

Whether a bare container owns Codex hooks, or whether a submodule should use
repository-wide hooks, is policy rather than a generic Git fact. That policy
must remain in Codex.

### Finding 2 — Blocker: preserving the common-directory caches misses the simplification

Status: **accepted**.

#### Plain-language explanation

Both packages repeatedly ask Git the same kind of question:

> Which Git metadata directory is shared by this repository's worktrees?

Running `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` starts a Git process, so each package
keeps its own notebook of previous answers:

- Session remembers one answer and the current working directory it belongs to.
- Checkpoint remembers several answers in a map keyed by worktree root.
- Each notebook needs a mutex so concurrent callers do not read it while it is
  being changed.
- Session also needs explicit clearing, largely so tests that change directory
  do not reuse an earlier answer.

In both packages, the effective flow is:

```text
Do I remember the answer?
    yes -> return it
    no  -> start Git, ask for the common directory, remember it, return it
```

The expensive part is starting Git, not interpreting the metadata. Once the
worktree root is known, the answer can be obtained by reading `.git` and its
optional `commondir` pointer directly. The proposed flow is therefore:

```text
Read the current Git metadata -> return the answer
```

That removes both notebooks, their locks, clearing behavior, cache-specific
tests, and the possibility of returning an answer made stale by repaired or
moved Git metadata. The separate worktree-root cache remains because locating
the root from an arbitrary current directory is still a real Git query.

Accepted decision: delete the session and checkpoint common-directory caches
after their subprocess traversal is replaced by direct, explicit-root metadata
reads. Retain the worktree-root discovery cache.

Current duplicate state:

- Session owns a process-global, CWD-keyed common-directory cache, its mutex,
  and `ClearGitCommonDirCache`.
- Checkpoint owns a process-global map keyed by worktree root plus another
  mutex and cache-specific cancellation tests.

These caches were introduced to avoid repeated
`git rev-parse --git-common-dir` subprocesses. Once common-directory resolution
becomes direct filesystem metadata traversal, the expected work is only:

- Normal checkout: stat `.git`; probe the absent `commondir`.
- Linked or separate layout: stat and read `.git`; read `commondir` when
  present.

Proposed final ownership:

```text
paths.WorktreeRoot
    owns the CWD -> worktree-root Git subprocess cache

gitrepo metadata resolution
    performs deterministic explicit-root filesystem reads with no cache
```

This would delete both common-directory caches, their locks and maps, cache
clearing, concurrent cold-miss behavior, invalidation questions, and
cache-specific cancellation behavior.

#### Verified performance evidence

The checkpoint cache's introducing commit, `637b802e8e`, records:

```text
git rev-parse fork: approximately 9.5 ms
checkpoint write:  approximately 12.9 ms
fork share:        approximately 73%
memoized speedup:  4.5x
```

A focused local M3 status benchmark was also run:

```text
cached:    approximately 22.1 ms/op average
no cache:  approximately 27.3 ms/op average
difference: approximately 5.3 ms/op
```

The benchmark was re-run on 2026-08-28 with three ten-iteration samples:

```text
cached average:       approximately 22.29 ms/op
uncached Git average: approximately 25.78 ms/op
difference:           approximately 3.49 ms/op
```

Those measurements prove that the Git subprocess is expensive. They do not
prove that direct filesystem resolution requires caching:

- Both comparisons are warm cache versus `git rev-parse`, not cache versus
  direct filesystem reads.
- The status benchmark retains the session cache across benchmark iterations,
  whereas an ordinary CLI invocation starts in a fresh process.
- The current tree has no checkpoint benchmark comparing cached and uncached
  filesystem metadata resolution.

The burden of proof therefore belongs to adding or retaining a metadata cache,
not to deleting the old subprocess workarounds.

#### Semantics that must be considered

1. **Cancellation:** a warm checkpoint cache currently succeeds with a
   cancelled context, while a cold Git subprocess fails. A context-free
   filesystem fact resolver would attempt the tiny reads regardless of
   cancellation. Higher-level operations should own workflow cancellation.
   Direct filesystem reads are not cancellable if a pathological filesystem
   blocks, which is a real trade-off.
2. **Git environment:** `git rev-parse` honors `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_WORK_TREE`, and
   `GIT_COMMON_DIR`. An explicit physical-root resolver should not. Hook paths
   generally benefit from avoiding inherited Git-environment contamination,
   but consumers that intentionally honor the environment must retain that
   behavior locally.
3. **Validation:** Git validates that it recognizes a repository. A filesystem
   parser validates only physical metadata. Required files and pointer formats
   must be checked, and consumers requiring genuine Git validation must retain
   a Git query.
4. **Staleness:** the caches assume a worktree's common directory cannot change
   during its lifetime. Repair, re-registration, root reuse, or manual metadata
   changes can invalidate that assumption. Direct reads observe current state
   rather than silently returning an old write target.
5. **Errors:** callers will receive metadata/filesystem errors instead of
   errors wrapping Git stderr. Diagnostics must remain clear even if exact
   error text changes.

Provisional Finding 2 conclusion:

> Delete the session and checkpoint common-directory caches after their
> subprocess traversal is replaced by explicit-root filesystem metadata
> resolution. Keep the existing worktree-root discovery cache. Do not add a
> new metadata cache without measurements.

### Finding 3 — Blocker: do not add policy flags to the resolver

Status: **accepted**.

#### Discussion note

The canonical resolver should answer one narrow question:

> What Git metadata is physically connected to this explicit worktree root?

It should not become a configurable decision engine such as:

```go
ResolveMetadata(root, ResolveOptions{
    CanonicalizeSymlinks: true,
    HonorGitEnvironment: false,
    ValidateBacklink:    true,
    RejectBare:          false,
})
```

Those switches look reusable but combine unrelated contracts. Every new
consumer or layout would create another supported option combination, its own
error behavior, and pressure to move consumer policy into `gitrepo`.

Concrete current differences prove that the policies are genuinely local:

- Codex canonicalizes symlinks, checks the linked-worktree `gitdir` backlink,
  distinguishes submodule and bare storage, verifies which checkout owns the
  common directory, and rejects roots that collide with `$HOME` or
  `$CODEX_HOME`. These checks decide where Codex may discover hooks safely.
- Manual session matching removes inherited Git repository overrides and
  resolves symlinks because it compares whether two recorded worktrees belong
  to the same physical repository.
- Session adopt asks Git for a combined top-level/common-directory answer and
  canonicalizes paths when deciding whether source and target stores are the
  same. That is user-invoked workflow policy, not metadata parsing.
- Trail reuse asks Git to validate an arbitrary existing path, its repository,
  and its branch. A filesystem metadata parser cannot replace that whole
  validation contract.

The fixed generic contract should instead:

- accept one explicit physical worktree root;
- return clean absolute paths;
- resolve relative `.git` and `commondir` pointers;
- validate the files and pointer formats required to produce the facts;
- preserve lexical symlink spelling;
- ignore `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_WORK_TREE`, and other environment overrides because it
  performs explicit-root filesystem reads;
- return physical facts without deciding hook ownership, trust, backlink
  health, or whether a layout is acceptable to a feature.

The important validation boundary is syntax and required metadata, not every
possible consistency policy. In particular, a stale worktree backlink may be a
reason for Codex to refuse a hook-root inference while another diagnostic may
still need the parsed common directory so it can explain or repair the layout.

Trade-off: policy consumers retain a small amount of deliberate local logic.
That duplication is preferable to a generic mode matrix because the decisions
have different meanings and failure semantics. It also prevents optional
symlink walks, backlink reads, or Git subprocesses from silently entering every
hot-path metadata lookup.

No relevant Entire checkpoint transcript is available locally. The environment
distinction is supported by commit-message evidence: hook-internal Git probes
must scrub inherited repository selectors, while user-invoked commands may
intentionally honor them. The remaining ownership analysis is inferred from
the current code and PR #2052 review history.

Accepted decision: use a single fixed physical resolver contract with all
feature policy left in its owning consumer. Do not add resolver options for
symlink canonicalization, Git environment handling, backlink validation, or
feature-specific acceptance policy.

Do not create a generic options surface for validation, symlink
canonicalization, Git environment handling, or backlink policy. The canonical
resolver should have one physical behavior:

- Accept an explicit physical worktree root.
- Return clean absolute paths.
- Resolve relative pointers.
- Validate required metadata.
- Preserve lexical symlink spelling.
- Ignore Git environment overrides.
- Avoid backlink, trust, ownership, or hook policy.

Special consumers retain their own real policy, including Codex backlink and
ownership checks, session-matching symlink equality, explicit-probe environment
isolation, adopt behavior, and trail validation.

### Finding 5 — High: no permanent compatibility-wrapper layer

Status: **accepted**.

A bad final state would keep all of these concepts as pass-throughs:

```text
session.GetGitCommonDir
strategy.GetGitCommonDir
checkpoint.resolveGitCommonDir
gitrepo.ResolveCommonGitPath
gitrepo.ResolveMetadata
```

Temporary wrappers may help an intermediate commit compile, but they must have
an explicit deletion stage. Final generic consumers should depend directly on
the canonical primitive.

#### Discussion note

A compatibility wrapper keeps an old name alive while forwarding to the new
implementation without adding a domain contract:

```go
func GetGitCommonDir(ctx context.Context) (string, error) {
    metadata, err := gitrepo.ResolveMetadata(...)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    return metadata.CommonDir, nil
}
```

Although this centralizes the calculation, it does not centralize ownership.
Future readers still see session, strategy, checkpoint, and gitrepo APIs that
all appear to own common-directory resolution. New callers can continue
depending on the wrong package, and consumer-specific behavior can later creep
back into a wrapper.

Current call sites show the cost clearly:

- settings, investigation, trail, review, session sweep, and strategy cleanup
  import `session.GetGitCommonDir` for a generic Git fact;
- setup and several strategy paths use `strategy.GetGitCommonDir`;
- three checkpoint paths use the private `resolveGitCommonDir`;
- Codex calls the exported `gitrepo.ResolveDotGitPath` and
  `ResolveCommonGitPath` separately, leaving composition and fallback semantics
  to the consumer.

All discovered production call sites are inside this repository. There is no
identified versioned external library contract that requires preserving these
exported names.

The important distinction is between a thin compatibility wrapper and a real
domain abstraction:

- `session.GetGitCommonDir` merely returns a generic Git fact and should go.
- A session state-store constructor may remain because it returns a session
  concept and owns session-specific storage and safety rules.
- A settings clone-preferences path helper may remain because it returns a
  settings-domain location, not generic repository metadata.

Private parsing helpers inside `gitrepo` may also remain when they make the
canonical implementation clearer. The prohibition is against preserving the
old public/package-level resolver surface, not against decomposing the one
canonical implementation internally.

Trade-off: removing wrappers makes the consolidation diff touch every internal
caller instead of offering a smaller mechanical migration. That broader local
edit is justified because changing the ownership graph is the purpose of this
work. Wrappers may exist temporarily between compiling commits, but the final
tree must delete them and their wrapper-specific tests.

No checkpoint transcript records a compatibility promise for these resolver
symbols. This conclusion is inferred from current call sites and package
boundaries.

Accepted decision: keep no compatibility wrappers in the final tree and
preferably avoid temporary wrappers as well. Retain only helpers that add
genuine domain meaning; private parsing helpers inside the canonical `gitrepo`
implementation are not compatibility wrappers.

## Blast-radius review — 2026-08-28

### Verdict

The consolidation has a wide call-site blast radius, but the serious failure
modes concentrate around two returned facts:

1. `CommonDir` routes repository-wide reads, writes, locks, and cleanup.
2. `WorktreeID` selects persistent session ownership and shadow-ref identity.

Findings 1 through 5 remain directionally sound if the canonical resolver is
all-or-error and former consumers preserve their local required-versus-
best-effort failure policy. Finding 6 remains provisional because an executed
symlink-valued `commondir` fixture disproved the proposed purely lexical
relationship comparison.

### Central safety invariant

> For every supported explicit worktree root, the resolver's Git directory and
> common directory must name the same physical directories Git uses. Missing,
> malformed, or non-directory required metadata must fail before the resolver
> returns any path a consumer could use as a write target.

This invariant is not yet proved for the proposed consolidation because no new
resolver exists. Executable probes reached strong baseline evidence for the
current primitives and exposed the gaps the eventual resolver must close.

### High-cost blast paths

- Session state is stored below `<common-dir>/entire-sessions`.
- Session advisory locks are stored below
  `<common-dir>/entire-session-locks`.
- Checkpoint queues, shadow-ref locks, redaction state, and loose-object cleanup
  derive targets from the same directory.
- Clone preferences, review markers, investigation state, trail state, and
  setup cleanup also derive locations from it.
- `WorktreeID` is persisted in session state and hashed into shadow-ref names.
  ID drift can make existing checkpoints appear missing or make worktrees
  collide without deleting the underlying refs.
- `gitrepo.OpenPath` uses the metadata paths to preserve object alternates and
  reftable behavior. Stricter resolver failure must not silently fall through
  to `git.PlainOpen`, which would appear to recover while losing those
  guarantees.

The highest-cost failure is therefore not a compile error. It is a plausible
but incorrect path that callers can successfully use to write into another
repository's shared metadata.

### Executed evidence

- The shipped low-level parsers matched Git's physical Git/common directories
  across real normal, conventional linked, relative-pointer, standard
  bare-backed linked, `.bare`-backed linked, separate-Git-dir, ordinary
  submodule, linked-submodule, linked-superproject-submodule, and moved/stale-
  backlink fixtures.
- A `.git` pointer to a missing registration was accepted by the shipped
  low-level parser while `git rev-parse` rejected the checkout. A canonical
  resolver must validate the resolved Git-directory target before treating an
  absent `commondir` as a healthy primary-repository fact.
- A valid linked worktree whose absolute `commondir` named a symlink alias was
  accepted by Git. The parser preserved the alias lexically, so comparing
  `parent(DotGitDir)` with `CommonDir/worktrees` as strings returned false even
  though the directories were physically identical.
- Focused baseline unit tests passed:
  `mise exec -- go test ./cmd/entire/cli/gitrepo ./cmd/entire/cli/paths -run
  'Test(OpenPath|HasObjectAlternates|GetWorktreeID)'`.
- The no-cost submodule/worktree integration baseline passed:
  `mise exec -- go test -tags=integration
  ./cmd/entire/cli/integration_test -run
  '^TestSubmoduleWorktree_SessionCreatesCheckpoint$'`.
- No paid agent E2E tests were run.

These tests prove current baseline behavior and the demonstrated hazards. They
do not prove the absent canonical resolver.

### Semantic risks to preserve deliberately

- **Required versus best effort:** session and checkpoint writes must stop on
  unresolved metadata; redaction, warnings, and similar optional paths must
  retain their current fail-open behavior.
- **Cancellation:** direct filesystem reads are context-free. Checkpoint queue
  persistence after ref creation must continue even when the initiating
  context has been cancelled.
- **Git environment:** an explicit-root resolver intentionally ignores
  inherited repository selectors. Genuine Git queries that intentionally
  validate user-selected repositories must not be replaced mechanically.
- **Symlink identity:** lexical paths may remain useful resolver output, but
  identity-sensitive relationships and session-lock convergence may require a
  narrowly scoped physical comparison.
- **Performance:** the resolver itself must launch no Git subprocess. Retain
  the worktree-root discovery cache, and prove representative hot hook paths do
  not gain subprocesses indirectly.
- **Ownership:** `gitrepo` already imports `paths`; retaining
  `paths.GetWorktreeID` as a forwarding wrapper would preserve the old seam or
  create import-cycle pressure.
- **Codex policy:** moved-worktree backlink, bare-container, submodule, trust,
  warning, diagnostic, and installation behavior remain Codex-owned policy.

### Risks checked and provisionally cleared

- No wire format, remote API, or database migration is implied.
- Deleting the two process caches removes in-memory memoization, not persistent
  repository data.
- Shared state remains under the repository common directory; the design does
  not require writing into a sibling checkout.
- Normal, linked, bare-backed, separate-Git-dir, and submodule layouts do not
  require a generic layout taxonomy.
- No external compatibility requirement was found for the old resolver names.

### Cheapest decisive merge proof

Add one real-Git table test in `gitrepo` that calls the shipped canonical
resolver and:

1. compares Git-directory and common-directory results with Git by physical
   identity across the full supported layout matrix;
2. asserts exact `WorktreeID` values, including the chosen symlink-alias rule;
3. proves missing or non-directory `gitdir` and `commondir` targets return no
   usable metadata;
4. proves derived write targets stay below the same physical common directory;
5. proves metadata resolution launches zero Git subprocesses; and
6. exercises malformed, alternates, and reftable repository opening so strict
   validation cannot silently downgrade through `git.PlainOpen`.

Retain focused consumer tests for cancellation-after-ref-write, required and
fail-open error behavior, mixed Git-environment operations, session-lock path
convergence, and Codex moved-backlink behavior. Deterministic filesystem and
Git fixtures are the appropriate proof; paid agent E2E is unnecessary.

### Finding 6 — High: derive worktree identity structurally

Status: **accepted with a physical-identity amendment**.

The relationship model remains promising, but the comparison cannot yet be
specified as raw lexical path equality. A valid symlink-valued `commondir`
counterexample makes a linked worktree look primary under that rule. Before
accepting this finding, the walkthrough chose narrowly scoped physical identity
for the relationship check. Do not canonicalize every returned metadata path
merely to solve this identity check.

Accepted decision: preserve the resolver's lexical `DotGitDir` and `CommonDir`
outputs, but derive `WorktreeID` by asking whether the parent of `DotGitDir` and
`CommonDir/worktrees` identify the same physical directory. If that identity
cannot be established, return an error rather than silently classifying a
linked worktree as primary. Do not add a resolver option for this behavior.

Proposed rule:

```text
registrationRoot = CommonDir/worktrees

if DotGitDir is an immediate child of registrationRoot:
    WorktreeID = basename(DotGitDir)
else:
    WorktreeID = empty
```

Examples:

| Layout | DotGitDir | CommonDir | ID |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Normal | `/repo/.git` | `/repo/.git` | empty |
| Conventional linked | `/repo/.git/worktrees/feature` | `/repo/.git` | `feature` |
| `.bare` linked | `/repo/.bare/worktrees/feature` | `/repo/.bare` | `feature` |
| Standard bare linked | `/repos/project.git/worktrees/feature` | `/repos/project.git` | `feature` |
| Separate Git directory, primary | `/storage/project` | `/storage/project` | empty |
| Ordinary submodule | `/super/.git/modules/library` | same | empty |
| Linked submodule | `/super/.git/modules/library/worktrees/feature` | `/super/.git/modules/library` | `feature` |

No `.git`, `.bare`, or `/modules/` marker branches should be necessary.

### Finding 7 — Medium: retain genuine Git queries

Status: **accepted**.

Do not delete subprocesses indiscriminately. Likely genuine Git queries include:

- Worktree-root discovery.
- Repository validation.
- `core.hooksPath` resolution.
- Adopt's combined root/common query until equivalent behavior is proven.
- Trail reuse validation for arbitrary paths.
- Manual session matching where environment isolation and symlink equality are
  part of the contract.

Accepted decision: replace Git subprocesses only when a caller already has an
explicit worktree root and needs physical `.git` or `commondir` facts. Retain
Git for worktree-root discovery, repository validation, configuration, ref and
branch resolution, and user-owned workflows whose environment behavior is
part of the contract. Do not measure success by deleting every
`rev-parse --git-common-dir` call.

### Finding 8 — High: repository opening must not downgrade after metadata failure

Status: **accepted**.

`gitrepo.OpenPath` currently attempts Entire's specialized repository opening,
checks whether object alternates require that path, and may then fall back to
plain go-git opening. The canonical resolver will become stricter than the
current low-level pointer parsers. A metadata-validation error must not be
converted into an apparently successful plain open that bypasses alternates
rewriting or reftable support.

Accepted decision: canonical metadata resolution and validation happen before
repository-opening fallback decisions. A metadata error remains fatal. Plain
opening is permitted only after positive evidence that the validated
repository does not require Entire's alternates or reftable handling; failure
to determine that is not evidence that fallback is safe. Preserve valid unusual
layouts through explicit tests rather than weakening validation globally.

### Finding 9 — High: centralize facts without centralizing failure policy

Status: **accepted**.

The canonical resolver should return one complete metadata result or an error.
It should not decide whether a session write must stop, a redaction cache may
disable itself, or a diagnostic should warn and continue. Those outcomes belong
to the consumer that understands the cost of proceeding without repository
metadata.

Accepted decision: the resolver returns one complete validated metadata result
or an error and has no optional, fail-open, or consumer-specific mode. Required
state writes and repository mutations stop; optional caches disable themselves;
warnings and diagnostics preserve their existing warn-or-skip behavior. Keep
these small policy branches in their owning packages rather than moving them
into `gitrepo`.

### Finding 10 — High: a bare container is not a worktree

Status: **accepted**.

A linked checkout backed by a standard bare repository has a worktree root and
ordinary `.git` pointer metadata, so the canonical worktree resolver must
support it. Passing the bare storage directory itself is different: it has no
`<root>/.git` because the root is the Git directory. Worktree metadata,
generic repository opening, and Codex's decision about hook ownership must not
collapse into one bare-layout special case.

Accepted decision: consolidate every physical traversal that starts from a
known checkout root and answers per-worktree Git directory, common directory,
or worktree identity. A linked checkout backed by bare storage uses that
canonical resolver. The bare storage directory itself has no worktree and is
handled by the separately validated repository-opening contract; Codex retains
its own bare-container hook policy. This is one owner per physical fact, not
one mega-function for every Git operation.

### Finding 11 — High: measure subprocesses at the operation boundary

Status: **accepted**.

It is not enough for the canonical metadata resolver itself to contain no Git
subprocess. A convenience API or migrated consumer could call
`paths.WorktreeRoot` after the operation already knows the root, or rediscover
it several times around metadata reads. That would preserve or increase hook
latency while making the resolver look locally efficient.

Accepted decision: the canonical resolver accepts an explicit root and never
performs root discovery. Callers that already know the root pass it directly;
only genuine CWD-based entry points call the retained cached
`paths.WorktreeRoot`. Verify Git subprocess counts across representative whole
hook operations, not merely by inspecting the resolver body. Metadata
consolidation must add no subprocesses and should remove the common-directory
forks it replaces.

### Finding 12 — High: lexical paths are not identity keys

Status: **accepted**.

The resolver will preserve lexical path spelling, but two different spellings
can name the same physical directory. Consumers that compare repositories,
deduplicate session locks, or establish multi-lock acquisition order must use
physical identity at that narrow boundary. Globally canonicalizing resolver
outputs would add cost and failure modes to every caller and would discard
useful diagnostic spelling.

Accepted decision: preserve cleaned absolute lexical paths in canonical
metadata. Use narrowly scoped physical identity when deriving worktree
identity, comparing repository ownership, deduplicating locks, or establishing
multi-lock order. If physical identity cannot be established at a safety-
critical boundary, return an error rather than treating the paths as different.
Do not globally canonicalize resolver output.

### Finding 13 — Medium: enforce the ownership boundary mechanically

Status: **accepted; required**.

Deleting four implementations does not prevent a future caller from adding a
new `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` cache or parsing `.git` independently.
Repository documentation and code review already failed to prevent this
fragmentation. A narrow source guard should keep deleted generic resolver names
absent and reject new common-directory subprocess traversal outside explicitly

The consolidation is necessary, but merely adding `WorktreeMetadata`,

The proposed code-judo move is:

## Structural findings

### Finding 1 — Blocker: fragmented ownership of Git metadata semantics

Status: **accepted**.

The central defect is not merely duplicated code. Several packages
independently decide what `.git`, `commondir`, and worktree identity mean.
Consequently, a fix in one resolver does not propagate to the others.

The generic layer should expose physical Git facts, not a growing `GitLayout`
taxonomy such as `Normal`, `Linked`, `Bare`, `DotBare`, `SeparateGitDir`,
`Submodule`, and `LinkedSubmodule`.

Provisional fact shape:

```go
type WorktreeMetadata struct {
    DotGitDir  string
    CommonDir  string
    WorktreeID string
}
```

Whether a bare container owns Codex hooks, or whether a submodule should use
repository-wide hooks, is policy rather than a generic Git fact. That policy
must remain in Codex.

### Finding 2 — Blocker: preserving the common-directory caches misses the simplification

Status: **accepted**.

#### Plain-language explanation

Both packages repeatedly ask Git the same kind of question:

> Which Git metadata directory is shared by this repository's worktrees?

Running `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` starts a Git process, so each package
keeps its own notebook of previous answers:

- Session remembers one answer and the current working directory it belongs to.
- Checkpoint remembers several answers in a map keyed by worktree root.
- Each notebook needs a mutex so concurrent callers do not read it while it is
  being changed.
- Session also needs explicit clearing, largely so tests that change directory
  do not reuse an earlier answer.

In both packages, the effective flow is:

```text
Do I remember the answer?
    yes -> return it
    no  -> start Git, ask for the common directory, remember it, return it
```

The expensive part is starting Git, not interpreting the metadata. Once the
worktree root is known, the answer can be obtained by reading `.git` and its
optional `commondir` pointer directly. The proposed flow is therefore:

```text
Read the current Git metadata -> return the answer
```

That removes both notebooks, their locks, clearing behavior, cache-specific
tests, and the possibility of returning an answer made stale by repaired or
moved Git metadata. The separate worktree-root cache remains because locating
the root from an arbitrary current directory is still a real Git query.

Accepted decision: delete the session and checkpoint common-directory caches
after their subprocess traversal is replaced by direct, explicit-root metadata
reads. Retain the worktree-root discovery cache.

Current duplicate state:

- Session owns a process-global, CWD-keyed common-directory cache, its mutex,
  and `ClearGitCommonDirCache`.
- Checkpoint owns a process-global map keyed by worktree root plus another
  mutex and cache-specific cancellation tests.

These caches were introduced to avoid repeated
`git rev-parse --git-common-dir` subprocesses. Once common-directory resolution
becomes direct filesystem metadata traversal, the expected work is only:

- Normal checkout: stat `.git`; probe the absent `commondir`.
- Linked or separate layout: stat and read `.git`; read `commondir` when
  present.

Proposed final ownership:

```text
paths.WorktreeRoot
    owns the CWD -> worktree-root Git subprocess cache

gitrepo metadata resolution
    performs deterministic explicit-root filesystem reads with no cache
```

This would delete both common-directory caches, their locks and maps, cache
clearing, concurrent cold-miss behavior, invalidation questions, and
cache-specific cancellation behavior.

The checkpoint cache's introducing commit, `637b802e8e`, records:

```text

checkpoint write:  approximately 12.9 ms
fork share:        approximately 73%
memoized speedup:  4.5x

A focused local M3 status benchmark was also run:

no cache:  approximately 27.3 ms/op average

uncached Git average: approximately 25.78 ms/op
difference:           approximately 3.49 ms/op

Those measurements prove that the Git subprocess is expensive. They do not
prove that direct filesystem resolution requires caching:

- Both comparisons are warm cache versus `git rev-parse`, not cache versus
  direct filesystem reads.
- The status benchmark retains the session cache across benchmark iterations,
  whereas an ordinary CLI invocation starts in a fresh process.
- The current tree has no checkpoint benchmark comparing cached and uncached

The burden of proof therefore belongs to adding or retaining a metadata cache,
not to deleting the old subprocess workarounds.

#### Semantics that must be considered

1. **Cancellation:** a warm checkpoint cache currently succeeds with a
   cancelled context, while a cold Git subprocess fails. A context-free
   filesystem fact resolver would attempt the tiny reads regardless of
   cancellation. Higher-level operations should own workflow cancellation.
   Direct filesystem reads are not cancellable if a pathological filesystem
   blocks, which is a real trade-off.
2. **Git environment:** `git rev-parse` honors `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_WORK_TREE`, and
   `GIT_COMMON_DIR`. An explicit physical-root resolver should not. Hook paths
   generally benefit from avoiding inherited Git-environment contamination,
   but consumers that intentionally honor the environment must retain that
   behavior locally.
3. **Validation:** Git validates that it recognizes a repository. A filesystem
   parser validates only physical metadata. Required files and pointer formats
   must be checked, and consumers requiring genuine Git validation must retain
   a Git query.
4. **Staleness:** the caches assume a worktree's common directory cannot change
   during its lifetime. Repair, re-registration, root reuse, or manual metadata
   changes can invalidate that assumption. Direct reads observe current state
   rather than silently returning an old write target.
5. **Errors:** callers will receive metadata/filesystem errors instead of
   errors wrapping Git stderr. Diagnostics must remain clear even if exact
   error text changes.

Status: **accepted**.

#### Discussion note

The canonical resolver should answer one narrow question:

> What Git metadata is physically connected to this explicit worktree root?

It should not become a configurable decision engine such as:

    CanonicalizeSymlinks: true,
    HonorGitEnvironment: false,
    ValidateBacklink:    true,
    RejectBare:          false,
})
```

error behavior, and pressure to move consumer policy into `gitrepo`.

Concrete current differences prove that the policies are genuinely local:

  distinguishes submodule and bare storage, verifies which checkout owns the
  common directory, and rejects roots that collide with `$HOME` or

- Manual session matching removes inherited Git repository overrides and

- Session adopt asks Git for a combined top-level/common-directory answer and

- Trail reuse asks Git to validate an arbitrary existing path, its repository,
  and its branch. A filesystem metadata parser cannot replace that whole
  validation contract.

The fixed generic contract should instead:

- accept one explicit physical worktree root;
- return clean absolute paths;
- resolve relative `.git` and `commondir` pointers;
- validate the files and pointer formats required to produce the facts;
- preserve lexical symlink spelling;
- ignore `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_WORK_TREE`, and other environment overrides because it
  performs explicit-root filesystem reads;
- return physical facts without deciding hook ownership, trust, backlink

The important validation boundary is syntax and required metadata, not every
possible consistency policy. In particular, a stale worktree backlink may be a

Refined acceptance criterion:

- affected consumer files shrink where their duplicate ownership is removed;
- `status.go` remains below 1,000 lines and preferably becomes materially
  smaller;
- no consumer gains new metadata policy or pass-through wrappers;
- metadata tests may grow substantially, but production code should show net

### Finding 5 — High: no permanent compatibility-wrapper layer

Status: **accepted**.

A bad final state would keep all of these concepts as pass-throughs:

```text
session.GetGitCommonDir
strategy.GetGitCommonDir
checkpoint.resolveGitCommonDir
gitrepo.ResolveCommonGitPath
gitrepo.ResolveMetadata
```

Temporary wrappers may help an intermediate commit compile, but they must have
an explicit deletion stage. Final generic consumers should depend directly on
the canonical primitive.

#### Discussion note

A compatibility wrapper keeps an old name alive while forwarding to the new
implementation without adding a domain contract:

```go
func GetGitCommonDir(ctx context.Context) (string, error) {
    metadata, err := gitrepo.ResolveMetadata(...)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    return metadata.CommonDir, nil
}
```

Although this centralizes the calculation, it does not centralize ownership.
Future readers still see session, strategy, checkpoint, and gitrepo APIs that
all appear to own common-directory resolution. New callers can continue
depending on the wrong package, and consumer-specific behavior can later creep
back into a wrapper.

Current call sites show the cost clearly:

- settings, investigation, trail, review, session sweep, and strategy cleanup
  import `session.GetGitCommonDir` for a generic Git fact;
- setup and several strategy paths use `strategy.GetGitCommonDir`;
- three checkpoint paths use the private `resolveGitCommonDir`;
- Codex calls the exported `gitrepo.ResolveDotGitPath` and
  `ResolveCommonGitPath` separately, leaving composition and fallback semantics
  to the consumer.

All discovered production call sites are inside this repository. There is no
identified versioned external library contract that requires preserving these
exported names.

The important distinction is between a thin compatibility wrapper and a real
domain abstraction:

- `session.GetGitCommonDir` merely returns a generic Git fact and should go.
- A session state-store constructor may remain because it returns a session
  concept and owns session-specific storage and safety rules.
- A settings clone-preferences path helper may remain because it returns a
  settings-domain location, not generic repository metadata.

Private parsing helpers inside `gitrepo` may also remain when they make the
canonical implementation clearer. The prohibition is against preserving the
old public/package-level resolver surface, not against decomposing the one
canonical implementation internally.

Trade-off: removing wrappers makes the consolidation diff touch every internal
caller instead of offering a smaller mechanical migration. That broader local
edit is justified because changing the ownership graph is the purpose of this
work. Wrappers may exist temporarily between compiling commits, but the final
tree must delete them and their wrapper-specific tests.

No checkpoint transcript records a compatibility promise for these resolver
symbols. This conclusion is inferred from current call sites and package
boundaries.

Accepted decision: keep no compatibility wrappers in the final tree and
preferably avoid temporary wrappers as well. Retain only helpers that add
genuine domain meaning; private parsing helpers inside the canonical `gitrepo`
implementation are not compatibility wrappers.

## Blast-radius review — 2026-08-28

### Verdict

The consolidation has a wide call-site blast radius, but the serious failure
modes concentrate around two returned facts:

1. `CommonDir` routes repository-wide reads, writes, locks, and cleanup.
2. `WorktreeID` selects persistent session ownership and shadow-ref identity.

Findings 1 through 5 remain directionally sound if the canonical resolver is
all-or-error and former consumers preserve their local required-versus-
best-effort failure policy. Finding 6 remains provisional because an executed
symlink-valued `commondir` fixture disproved the proposed purely lexical
relationship comparison.

### Central safety invariant

> For every supported explicit worktree root, the resolver's Git directory and
> common directory must name the same physical directories Git uses. Missing,
> malformed, or non-directory required metadata must fail before the resolver
> returns any path a consumer could use as a write target.

This invariant is not yet proved for the proposed consolidation because no new
resolver exists. Executable probes reached strong baseline evidence for the
current primitives and exposed the gaps the eventual resolver must close.

### High-cost blast paths

- Session state is stored below `<common-dir>/entire-sessions`.
- Session advisory locks are stored below
  `<common-dir>/entire-session-locks`.
- Checkpoint queues, shadow-ref locks, redaction state, and loose-object cleanup
  derive targets from the same directory.
- Clone preferences, review markers, investigation state, trail state, and
  setup cleanup also derive locations from it.
- `WorktreeID` is persisted in session state and hashed into shadow-ref names.
  ID drift can make existing checkpoints appear missing or make worktrees
  collide without deleting the underlying refs.
- `gitrepo.OpenPath` uses the metadata paths to preserve object alternates and
  reftable behavior. Stricter resolver failure must not silently fall through
  to `git.PlainOpen`, which would appear to recover while losing those
  guarantees.

The highest-cost failure is therefore not a compile error. It is a plausible
but incorrect path that callers can successfully use to write into another
repository's shared metadata.

### Executed evidence

- The shipped low-level parsers matched Git's physical Git/common directories
  across real normal, conventional linked, relative-pointer, standard
  bare-backed linked, `.bare`-backed linked, separate-Git-dir, ordinary
  submodule, linked-submodule, linked-superproject-submodule, and moved/stale-
  backlink fixtures.
- A `.git` pointer to a missing registration was accepted by the shipped
  low-level parser while `git rev-parse` rejected the checkout. A canonical
  resolver must validate the resolved Git-directory target before treating an
  absent `commondir` as a healthy primary-repository fact.
- A valid linked worktree whose absolute `commondir` named a symlink alias was
  accepted by Git. The parser preserved the alias lexically, so comparing
  `parent(DotGitDir)` with `CommonDir/worktrees` as strings returned false even
  though the directories were physically identical.
- Focused baseline unit tests passed:
  `mise exec -- go test ./cmd/entire/cli/gitrepo ./cmd/entire/cli/paths -run
  'Test(OpenPath|HasObjectAlternates|GetWorktreeID)'`.
- The no-cost submodule/worktree integration baseline passed:
  `mise exec -- go test -tags=integration
  ./cmd/entire/cli/integration_test -run
  '^TestSubmoduleWorktree_SessionCreatesCheckpoint$'`.
- No paid agent E2E tests were run.

These tests prove current baseline behavior and the demonstrated hazards. They
do not prove the absent canonical resolver.

### Semantic risks to preserve deliberately

- **Required versus best effort:** session and checkpoint writes must stop on
  unresolved metadata; redaction, warnings, and similar optional paths must
  retain their current fail-open behavior.
- **Cancellation:** direct filesystem reads are context-free. Checkpoint queue
  persistence after ref creation must continue even when the initiating
  context has been cancelled.
- **Git environment:** an explicit-root resolver intentionally ignores
  inherited repository selectors. Genuine Git queries that intentionally
  validate user-selected repositories must not be replaced mechanically.
- **Symlink identity:** lexical paths may remain useful resolver output, but
  identity-sensitive relationships and session-lock convergence may require a
  narrowly scoped physical comparison.
- **Performance:** the resolver itself must launch no Git subprocess. Retain
  the worktree-root discovery cache, and prove representative hot hook paths do
  not gain subprocesses indirectly.
- **Ownership:** `gitrepo` already imports `paths`; retaining
  `paths.GetWorktreeID` as a forwarding wrapper would preserve the old seam or
  create import-cycle pressure.
- **Codex policy:** moved-worktree backlink, bare-container, submodule, trust,
  warning, diagnostic, and installation behavior remain Codex-owned policy.

### Risks checked and provisionally cleared

- No wire format, remote API, or database migration is implied.
- Deleting the two process caches removes in-memory memoization, not persistent
  repository data.
- Shared state remains under the repository common directory; the design does
  not require writing into a sibling checkout.
- Normal, linked, bare-backed, separate-Git-dir, and submodule layouts do not
  require a generic layout taxonomy.
- No external compatibility requirement was found for the old resolver names.

### Cheapest decisive merge proof

Add one real-Git table test in `gitrepo` that calls the shipped canonical
resolver and:

1. compares Git-directory and common-directory results with Git by physical
   identity across the full supported layout matrix;
2. asserts exact `WorktreeID` values, including the chosen symlink-alias rule;
3. proves missing or non-directory `gitdir` and `commondir` targets return no
   usable metadata;
4. proves derived write targets stay below the same physical common directory;
5. proves metadata resolution launches zero Git subprocesses; and
6. exercises malformed, alternates, and reftable repository opening so strict
   validation cannot silently downgrade through `git.PlainOpen`.

Retain focused consumer tests for cancellation-after-ref-write, required and
fail-open error behavior, mixed Git-environment operations, session-lock path
convergence, and Codex moved-backlink behavior. Deterministic filesystem and
Git fixtures are the appropriate proof; paid agent E2E is unnecessary.

### Finding 6 — High: derive worktree identity structurally

Status: **accepted with a physical-identity amendment**.

The relationship model remains promising, but the comparison cannot yet be
specified as raw lexical path equality. A valid symlink-valued `commondir`
counterexample makes a linked worktree look primary under that rule. Before
accepting this finding, the walkthrough chose narrowly scoped physical identity
for the relationship check. Do not canonicalize every returned metadata path
merely to solve this identity check.

Accepted decision: preserve the resolver's lexical `DotGitDir` and `CommonDir`
outputs, but derive `WorktreeID` by asking whether the parent of `DotGitDir` and
`CommonDir/worktrees` identify the same physical directory. If that identity
cannot be established, return an error rather than silently classifying a
linked worktree as primary. Do not add a resolver option for this behavior.

Proposed rule:

```text
registrationRoot = CommonDir/worktrees

if DotGitDir is an immediate child of registrationRoot:
    WorktreeID = basename(DotGitDir)
else:
    WorktreeID = empty
```

Examples:

| Layout | DotGitDir | CommonDir | ID |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Normal | `/repo/.git` | `/repo/.git` | empty |
| Conventional linked | `/repo/.git/worktrees/feature` | `/repo/.git` | `feature` |
| `.bare` linked | `/repo/.bare/worktrees/feature` | `/repo/.bare` | `feature` |
| Standard bare linked | `/repos/project.git/worktrees/feature` | `/repos/project.git` | `feature` |
| Separate Git directory, primary | `/storage/project` | `/storage/project` | empty |
| Ordinary submodule | `/super/.git/modules/library` | same | empty |
| Linked submodule | `/super/.git/modules/library/worktrees/feature` | `/super/.git/modules/library` | `feature` |

No `.git`, `.bare`, or `/modules/` marker branches should be necessary.

### Finding 7 — Medium: retain genuine Git queries

Status: **accepted**.

Do not delete subprocesses indiscriminately. Likely genuine Git queries include:

- Worktree-root discovery.
- Repository validation.
- `core.hooksPath` resolution.
- Adopt's combined root/common query until equivalent behavior is proven.
- Trail reuse validation for arbitrary paths.
- Manual session matching where environment isolation and symlink equality are
  part of the contract.

Accepted decision: replace Git subprocesses only when a caller already has an
explicit worktree root and needs physical `.git` or `commondir` facts. Retain
Git for worktree-root discovery, repository validation, configuration, ref and
branch resolution, and user-owned workflows whose environment behavior is
part of the contract. Do not measure success by deleting every
`rev-parse --git-common-dir` call.

### Finding 8 — High: repository opening must not downgrade after metadata failure

Status: **accepted**.

`gitrepo.OpenPath` currently attempts Entire's specialized repository opening,
checks whether object alternates require that path, and may then fall back to
plain go-git opening. The canonical resolver will become stricter than the
current low-level pointer parsers. A metadata-validation error must not be
converted into an apparently successful plain open that bypasses alternates
rewriting or reftable support.

Accepted decision: canonical metadata resolution and validation happen before
repository-opening fallback decisions. A metadata error remains fatal. Plain
opening is permitted only after positive evidence that the validated
repository does not require Entire's alternates or reftable handling; failure
to determine that is not evidence that fallback is safe. Preserve valid unusual
layouts through explicit tests rather than weakening validation globally.

### Finding 9 — High: centralize facts without centralizing failure policy

Status: **accepted**.

The canonical resolver should return one complete metadata result or an error.
It should not decide whether a session write must stop, a redaction cache may
disable itself, or a diagnostic should warn and continue. Those outcomes belong
to the consumer that understands the cost of proceeding without repository
metadata.

Accepted decision: the resolver returns one complete validated metadata result
or an error and has no optional, fail-open, or consumer-specific mode. Required
state writes and repository mutations stop; optional caches disable themselves;
warnings and diagnostics preserve their existing warn-or-skip behavior. Keep
these small policy branches in their owning packages rather than moving them
into `gitrepo`.

### Finding 10 — High: a bare container is not a worktree

Status: **accepted**.

A linked checkout backed by a standard bare repository has a worktree root and
ordinary `.git` pointer metadata, so the canonical worktree resolver must
support it. Passing the bare storage directory itself is different: it has no
`<root>/.git` because the root is the Git directory. Worktree metadata,
generic repository opening, and Codex's decision about hook ownership must not
collapse into one bare-layout special case.

Accepted decision: consolidate every physical traversal that starts from a
known checkout root and answers per-worktree Git directory, common directory,
or worktree identity. A linked checkout backed by bare storage uses that
canonical resolver. The bare storage directory itself has no worktree and is
handled by the separately validated repository-opening contract; Codex retains
its own bare-container hook policy. This is one owner per physical fact, not
one mega-function for every Git operation.

### Finding 11 — High: measure subprocesses at the operation boundary

Status: **accepted**.

It is not enough for the canonical metadata resolver itself to contain no Git
subprocess. A convenience API or migrated consumer could call
`paths.WorktreeRoot` after the operation already knows the root, or rediscover
it several times around metadata reads. That would preserve or increase hook
latency while making the resolver look locally efficient.

Accepted decision: the canonical resolver accepts an explicit root and never
performs root discovery. Callers that already know the root pass it directly;
only genuine CWD-based entry points call the retained cached
`paths.WorktreeRoot`. Verify Git subprocess counts across representative whole
hook operations, not merely by inspecting the resolver body. Metadata
consolidation must add no subprocesses and should remove the common-directory
forks it replaces.

### Finding 12 — High: lexical paths are not identity keys

Status: **accepted**.

The resolver will preserve lexical path spelling, but two different spellings
can name the same physical directory. Consumers that compare repositories,
deduplicate session locks, or establish multi-lock acquisition order must use
physical identity at that narrow boundary. Globally canonicalizing resolver
outputs would add cost and failure modes to every caller and would discard
useful diagnostic spelling.

Accepted decision: preserve cleaned absolute lexical paths in canonical
metadata. Use narrowly scoped physical identity when deriving worktree
identity, comparing repository ownership, deduplicating locks, or establishing
multi-lock order. If physical identity cannot be established at a safety-
critical boundary, return an error rather than treating the paths as different.
Do not globally canonicalize resolver output.

### Finding 13 — Medium: enforce the ownership boundary mechanically

Status: **accepted; required**.

Deleting four implementations does not prevent a future caller from adding a
new `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` cache or parsing `.git` independently.
Repository documentation and code review already failed to prevent this
fragmentation. A narrow source guard should keep deleted generic resolver names
absent and reject new common-directory subprocess traversal outside explicitly
audited semantic Git queries.

Accepted decision: add a narrow mechanical guard after migration. It must keep
the deleted generic resolver surface absent and reject new
`rev-parse --git-common-dir` traversal outside a small audited list of genuine
semantic Git queries. Do not broadly ban `.git`, `commondir`, or `rev-parse`
strings because tests and policy consumers have legitimate uses.

### Finding 14 — High: real Git layouts are the executable specification

Status: **accepted**.

Handwritten pointer fixtures are useful for malformed metadata, but they can
encode impossible Git layouts and prove only that code agrees with the test
author. Valid-layout coverage should create repositories through Git and
compare the shipped resolver with Git's physical answers. Handwritten fixtures
should be reserved for broken states Git will not create intentionally.

Accepted decision: use Git-created, isolated repositories as the executable
specification for every valid layout. Compare resolver paths with Git by
physical identity and assert exact agreed worktree IDs. Use handwritten
fixtures only for malformed or broken states, and require those cases to return
no usable metadata. Retain focused consumer agreement, failure-policy,
repository-opening, ownership-guard, and whole-operation subprocess tests. No
paid agent E2E is required.

## Walkthrough closeout

Status on 2026-08-28: **all material design findings discussed and accepted**.

Implementation remains unapproved. Before changing production code, obtain an
explicit user instruction to begin implementation. The accepted constraints
remain binding: keep the change inside the `gitrepo` ownership boundary and
its existing consumers, preserve Codex and bare-repository policy, retain
genuine Git queries, delete obsolete caches and wrappers, shrink former owner
modules, add the real-layout proof and narrow ownership guard, and do not run
paid agent E2E tests.

## Provisional target architecture

```text
paths
└── WorktreeRoot(ctx)

gitrepo
├── canonical explicit-root metadata facts
└── repository opening consumes the same facts

generic consumers
├── session state locations
├── checkpoint refs, queues, and redaction
├── settings preferences
├── review and investigation metadata
├── shallow-file and status metadata
└── strategy state and locks

policy consumers
├── Codex ownership, backlink, trust, and diagnostics

```

- No implementation during the guided walkthrough without explicit approval.
- Do not reintroduce automatic writes from one worktree into another checkout.
- Do not broaden the work into hook-writer hardening or settings
  reserialization.
- Do not change Codex diagnostics, warnings, trust behavior, or installation
  semantics.
- Do not preserve accidental complexity merely for source compatibility.
- Avoid unrelated cleanup.
- Do not run paid agent E2E tests unless explicitly requested.
- Do not push, merge, create or close issues or PRs, label, or post public

- Require net structural simplification and preferably net production-code

- Reject layout enums, resolver option flags, unmeasured metadata caches,
  permanent compatibility wrappers, generic Codex policy, and disguised
  path-marker detection.

paths.WorktreeRoot(ctx)          known explicit root
